WANTED: CHIEF ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICER
PSI UPSILON FRATERNITY
Location of Position: Two Station Square
Paoli, Pennsylvania 19301
Title of Position: Executive Director
Salary: Based upon experience of person selected
Benefits: Health insurance, annual and sick/disability leave, retirement pro
gram.
Responsibilities:
(1) Under the direction of the Executive Council, implements resolutions
adopted at annual Conventions, all decisions and directives for the Executive
Council, and established policies and procedures.
(2) Operates Fraternity headquarters office, including recommendation of
appointment of Field Directors, appointment of all other staff members (with
the concurrence ofthe President); assignment and delegation of responsibilities
to staff members; setting salaries for all staff within ranges determined annually
by the Executive Council; and termination of staff members when appropriate.
(3) Oversees the operation of each Chapter, visits as many chapters as pos
sible annually, and responds to critical needs as they arise.
(4) Serves as primary link with alumni, assists in the establishment and
operation of alumni organizations, and conducts the Annual Giving Program.
(5) Organizes the Annual Convention, arranges and prepares agendas for
the Executive Council with approval of the President, directs expansion un
dertakings, and represents the Fraternity in interfraternity activities and public
affairs as authorized by the Executive Council.
Minimum Qualifications:
(1) Bachelor's degree from college or university.
(2) At least four years experience in supervision and management, trade or
professional associations, public relations, fund-raising, or similar people-re
lated activity.
(3) Demonstrated commitment to voluntary organizations, particularly fra
ternities and sororities.
(4) Willingness and abihty to travel extensively as required.
SEND RESUME (with names, addresses and current telephone numbers of
all current and prior employers and at least three references who are not
employers) WITH COVER LETTER DESCRIBING YOUR INTEREST IN

VV hen I last wrote to you about our
search for an Executive Director, it was
under positive and indeed encouraging
circumstances �
the expansion of the
Fraternity's efforts to improve service to
our
chapters and alumni organizations and
the exciting prospect of a full-time Foun
dation office that would build the endow
ment of the Foundation and thus further
the educational programs and efforts of
the Fraternity.
On this occasion, however, I am writ
ing again about the search for a new Ex
ecutive Director as a result of the tragic
death of Kathy McGlone, our Executive
Director from October 5, 1987, until Au
gust 19, 1989. Her long and valiant strug
gle with a rare form of leukemia ended
on the last day of the Fraternity's Con
vention in Chicago and substantially
dampened the normally positive atmos
phere that traditionally prevails at such
an event. Kathy's many contributions to
the Fraternity, her family, and her com
munity are noted elsewhere in this issue
of The Diamond and will provide you with
a good sense of the loss we all feel with
ber passing.
This tragic event necessitates the re
newal of our search for an Executive Di
rector to serve as the chief administrative
officer of the Fraternity. We are seeking
applications from anyone who might meet
the requirements indicated in the accom
panying search announcement.
We are
particularly enthusiastic about
the challenges that a new Executive Di
rector of Psi Upsilon will face. Psi Up
silon is now reaching a point when we
can
again turn our attention to expansion
into other campuses while we adjust in
ternally to the enormous pressures cre
ated by the need to manage carefully our
positive programs, while still assuring that
any risks associated with these programs
are minimized or eliminated altogether.
The challenges to the pledging process,
the need to reassess the methods by which
we achieve and transmit brotherhood, the
tremendous opportunities for leadership
development �
all are challenges facing
us in the immediate future and will re
quire the services of an energetic, ca
pable administrator who is willing to rec
ommend often tough options to the
President and Executive Council and then
implement the decisions that result from
discussion of such recommendations.
I urge all who read this to consider
carefully those who you believe may be
eligible for such a position. Please urge
appropriate candidates (including your
self) to send their resumes to me at the
earliest possible moment. Our aim is to
carefrilly and thoroughly conduct this
search in a way that will assure prompt
and effective continuity in this crucial po
sition. I look forward to your continuing
and thoughtful assistance in this impor
tant process.
Yours in the bonds
William R .
Robie,

DELTA CHAPTER DECLARED
INACTIVE
(Chicago, IL) At their meeting held in
conjunction with the 146th Convention,
the Executive Council of Psi Upsilon,
based upon recommendation from the
Delta Corporation, relegated the Delta
Chapter to inactive status.
The action of the Executive Council
came after a four-month investigation by
New York University, with the cooper
ation of the Delta Alumni Corporation,
the fraternity staff, and the Executive
Council. Through this investigation. New
York University found reason to believe
that there was significant drug use in the
chapter. As a result of their findings. New
York University suspended the Chapter
for two years.
Following several unsuccessful at
tempts by the Delta Alumni Corporation
to work with the undergraduates of the
Delta, the Delta Alumni Corporation
reached the same conclusion. The Delta
Alumni Corporation presented a formal
request to the Executive Council to de
clare the chapter inactive at the August
17, 1989 meeting.
Working in cooperation with the New
York University officials, Psi Upsilon is
confident that the Delta chapter will be
reactivated as soon as possible. Psi Up
silon has been proudly represented with
a chapter at NYU since 1837, and it brings
great sorrow to the entire fraternity, par
ticularly to the Delta alumni, to no longer
have the chapter active.
PROPOSITION EIGHT
ELIMINATES TKE PLEDGING
(Indianapolis, IN) The future of the
"pledging" process is being discussed a
great deal these days. At the Tau Kappa
Epsilon Conclave in August, the talk both
in and out of every meeting and meal
focused upon Proposition Eight, the leg
islation to eliminate pledging from the
280 TKE chapters nationwide.
Although Zeta Beta Tau was the first
fraternity to eliminate pledging, Tau
Kappa Epsilon is the first to have the
measure enacted by a vote of undergrad
uate chapters. (The ZBT action was dehvered independent ofa chapter vote but
within the authority of its Supreme
Council.)
In addressing a news conference in In
dianapolis, immediate past intemational
TKE president Bruce Melchert an
nounced, "TKE hopes to provide the
leadership for all fraternities to take sim
ilar actions." The TKE Membership De
velopment Program vidU be phased in over
the next two years with mandatory com
pliance by September 1, 1991. Several
chapters will pilot the program this fall.
Three levels of fraternal achievement
will encompass the undergraduate ex
perience. Within approximately 14 days
of bid acceptance and following an inter
view with a Membership Quality Board,
new members will be initiated into the
first order. Members in good standing at
the conclusion of the junior year will be
inducted into the second order, and all
members upon graduation will gain ad
mission into the final order called the
"Fraternity for Life."
Eileen Stevens, whose son died of acute
alcohol poisoning during a hazing inci
dent at Alfred University (NY) and who
is the founder of CHUCK �
Committee
to Halt Useless College Killings, ad
dressed the TKE Conclave opening ban
quet, "Whenever you have a two-tiered
system where there are members and
pledges, the opportunity for hazing per
sists. TKE can take the lead in removing
that opportunity."
Tau Kappa Epsilon and Zeta Beta Tau
have received considerable publicity for
their actions in The New York Times, USA
Today, and the "Today" television pro
gram, as well as many local papers.
PARTIES NO LONGER A RIGHT
BUT A PRIVILEGE AT
WASHINGTON STATE
(Pullman, WA) The Washington State
University IFC passed landmark legis
lation by a vote of 24-1 to suspend chap
ter social privileges for two weeks for
every 0.05 points that the organization's
grade point average falls below the allmen's undergraduate average. The pol
icy will become effective Spring Semes
ter 1990 based upon the academic rank
ings for the fall term.
Just as a standard exists for initiation
eligibility at Washington State; fratemi
ties leaders decided that a standard was
necessary for social eligibility. Social
privileges would become a positive in
centive for those members previously not
inspired to achieve academic success nor
spend time studying.
TOUGH NEW DRINKING LAWS
(Columbus, OH and Seattle, WA) The
states of Ohio and Washington both
passed strict new legislation on July 1,
1989, focusing on underage drinking. The
ramifications of these measures are sure
to have an impact on college campuses,
where the majority of students are not
yet of legal drinking age.
Legislation signed into law in Ohio
states that it is a crime for the ovraer of
private property to allow anyone under
21 to remain on the property while con
suming or possessing alcoholic bever
ages. Penalties for violating the new law
can include six months imprisonment, a
$1,000 fine, and five years probation.
In Washington, a new keg registration
law took efiiect to send a warning to adults
who might provide beer to people under
21. The state law places responsibility for
dispensing the beer on the keg's buyer.
It requires a buyer to enter into a written
promise, under penalty of perjury, that
be or she will not serve minors.
Kegs will come with a sticker that in
cludes a declaration form. Buyers must
write on the form that they are at least
21 and will not allow anyone under 21 to
drink from the keg. They must include
their name and address on the form and
the address at which the beer is con
sumed. Then they must sign the form.
The sticker and form will be attached near
the top and at the side of the keg so the
message is clear to party-goers.
The system provides a paper trail. H
the police were to enter a party and find
kegs and underage drinkers, they will
know who purchased the alcohol. Any
one
furnishing liquor to a minor can be
fined up to $500, jailed for a month, or
both.

EXPANSION: BROADENING THE
"CHOSEN FEW"
(Paoli, PA) With the addition ofthe Kappa
Phi Chapter at Pennsylvania State Uni
versity to Psi Upsilon's roll, Psi U is once
again looking at potential sites for future
growth. Our history is one of very con
servative expansion. While that does not
mean we can expand only a few times a
century, it does mean that any expansion
we undertake must be to a school of ex
cellent reputation with a
group of out
standing undergraduates. The Interna
tional Office constantly reviews expansion
possibilities and checks into any leads.
But undergraduates and alumni can assist
in this responsibility. We are
always in
terested in learning of any children of
alumni, or
siblings of current undergrad
uates, or any other relatives or friends of
members, attending schools where Psi
Upsilon is not represented. Further
more, many alumni live near
college
campuses or even work for schools and
could be of enormous assistance in start
ing a new
chapter. No one will ask for
more
help than you are able to give. But
if you have any ideas or would like to
learn more about Psi Upsilon's expansion
plans, please contact the International
Office.
SPEAKING OF THE FOUNDATION
The First Thirty Years (Continued)
Webster defines a "foundation" as "funds given for the permanent
support of an institution." And so it w^as in 1958 when The Psi Upsilon
Foundation, Inc. was first conceived and established. A key word in
that definition is "permanent." Psi Upsilon Fraternity, already 125 years
old at that juncture, is a lasting brotherhood �
extending in perpetuity.
Permanency also reflects the policy of the Foundation's Directors from
the outset to utilize income only and to maintain intact all contributed
funds, except for expenditures to further increase the principal.
In our last two installments we talked of establishing the Foundation,
ofthe stated purposes in its Articles of Incorporation, of its slow growth
initially, of embarking early on a
scholarship assistance program, and of
launching the Sesquicentennial Fund in 1981. Now let's take a look at
how we laid the base for this considerable undertaking.
With the guidance of Edward K. Dorris, a professional fundraiser,
the officers of both the Fraternity and the Foundation began to shape
objectives, format, and procedures. Vital to the success of our venture
were;
(1) An understanding that the Sesquicentennial Fund is a program,
not a
campaign. Unlike the fund-raising endeavors of colleges, hospitals,
and churches, which typically are intensive, of limited duration, and
followed by successive undertakings, ours has been tailored to the
uniqueness of a
fraternity as more of a
low-key, long-term, one-time
undertaking.
(2) The development of a considered and compelling case statement.
This involved a careful projection of Psi Upsilon's near-range and longrange needs, as well as a balance of opportunities which can appeal to
our varied member constituency.
(3) An agreement on continuing and enhancing the Fraternity's Annual
Giving program throughout the Sesquicentennial Fund's solicitation pe
riod. One of the few, if not the only. Annual Giving programs in the
firatemity world supporting approximately one-half the operating budget,
this uninterrupted appeal has been deemed essential to the ongoing
activities of Psi Upsilon. Though Annual Giving contributions are not
tax deductible, involvement by a large segment of our alumni body is
a source of incalculable strength.
(4) The conversion ofthe Foundation's status from a private foundation
to a public charity. This move was designed to lessen the operating
restrictions placed on the Psi Upsilon Foundation and to broaden the
terms of accepting contributions. Following a five-year test period, dur
ing which the Foundation was permitted to operate as a public foun
dation, a final determination letter of approval was received from the
Internal Revenue Service in 1986.
Now the stage was set. We were ready to invite participation. See
our next installment for how it played.
Henry B .
Poor, Gamma '39
Foundation Executive Director

Psi Upsilon Mourns
the Loss of
Kathleen M. McGlone
By
Mark D. Bauer, Omega 83
Thomas L. Phillips, Omicron '85
and Terrence J. Turner, Beta Beta '88
X si Upsilon has lost one of our truly great ones. Kathleen M.
McGlone, Lambda '82H, Psi Upsilon's Executive Director,
passed away on August 19, 1989. She was 42 years old and
recovering from a bone marrow transplant, undertaken in a
final attempt to win her battle with leukemia, at the Johns
Hopkins University Hospital.
It is difficult to reduce to print a description of one of the
most remarkable human beings who ever lived. Fortunately,
in the years that Kathy was a member of the Psi Upsilon staff,
she was able to meet and impact upon the lives ofthe thousands
of undergraduates and alumni whom she met. Serving on the
staff for over eleven years, and as Executive Director for the
last two, Kathy made Psi U her second family, and devoted a
considerable amount of her life bringing Psi Upsilon to where
it is today. This article is dedicated to preserve her memory
for those who will never be able to meet her.
Kathy grew up in Drexel Hill, Pennsylvania, a lovely suburb
of Philadelphia. It was there with her parents, John and Alice
Hendrick, three sisters, and a brother, that Kathy was exposed
to the love, honor, integrity, and sincerity that became such
an integral part of her personality. Upon graduating from the
Academy of Notre Dame, in Villanova, Pennsylvania, Kathy
enrolled at Gwynned Mercy College in the Philadephia sub
urbs. While attending college, Kathy married Gerard Mc
Glone. Over the next several years, Kathy and Jerry had three
children: Jerry, Jr., Sean, and Chris. By 1978
Kathy felt that the children were old enough for her to get a
part-time job. The position she choose turned out to be parttime in theory only, and it certainly became much more than
just a job. Psi Upsilon is truly blessed that Kathy decided to
join the staff of the International Office in Paoli.
From the start, Kathy gave the position of Records Secretary
much more than the average person. Psi Upsilon was one of
the very last fratemities to estabUsh an administrative office.
As a result, a tremendous amount of work had to be done just
to bring the Fratemity into the 20th Century. As Henry B.
Poor's assistant, indeed partner, Kathy also filled the role of
financial manager and jack-of-all-trades. Because of her out
standing abilities and tireless devotion, the position of Director
of Publications and Services was created for Kathy in 1981. In
that position, Kathy became editor of The Diamond. As such,
Kathy became the first woman in history to work for a college
fratemity in a professional capacity.
Kathy's contributions to The Diamond were extraordinary.
As Editor, she brought the publication on to a timely schedule
for the first time in many years. She also pubhshed three award
winning articles and completely transformed the design of The
Diamond into the modem publication you hold today.
While assisting in the organization of the 139th Convention
at the Lambda Chapter in 1982, Kathy played a role in the
reinvigoration of that Chapter's alumni association. She de
veloped a strong rapport with the undergraduates and alumni
of the Lambda. Soon after the Convention, the Lambda in-

of PSI UPSILON 5
quired as to whether they might have the singular honor of
initiating Kathy into Psi Upsilon. Kathy was delighted to accept
and was initiated into our fraternity in the fall of 1982.
In conjunction with the Psi Upsilon Foundation's Susquicentennial Fund Drive, Henry Poor had to devote increasing
amounts of time to fund raising activities. Accordingly, Kathy
was named Psi U's first Administrative Director in 1983. As
such, Kathy was given responsibility for the day-to-day oper
ations ofthe International Office. In 1987, Kathy became Ex
ecutive Director of the Fraternity when Henry moved on to
become the first fiill-time Executive Director ofthe Psi Upsilon
Foundation.
In 1985 Kathy learned that she had a rare form of leukemia.
Indeed, it was so rare that her doctors could not even develop
any reasonable prognosis. Rather than dwell on
something that
would probably destroy the life of a lesser person, Kathy just
ignored it and went on. Since 1985, she had never entirely felt
herself. There were many days that she was weak, or her legs
swelled, or she was feverish. But no one ever knew that except
Kathy. She ignored her personal misfortune and fought on.
She did not allow her illness to keep her from being a model
mother and wife, or from executing her duties to Psi Upsilon.
In May of this year the doctors changed the diagnosis of her
disease to a more common form of leukemia, but unfortunately
one that can only be cured through a very risky and painful
bone marrow transplant. Kathy was faced with the rigorous
treatment plan, or almost certain death. Kathy faced death as
she faced life; bravely and with unceasing care and concern for
others. On Saturday, August 19, Kathy died from complications
of the bone marrow transplant. Ironically, less than one hour
before her death. Brother Michael L. Huffman, Zeta '77, Mas
ter of Ceremonies at the 146th Convention banquet in Chicago,
had made a toast to Brother McGlone, wishing her swift and
complete recovery.
Executive Council President William R. Robie, Epsilon
Omega '66, made the sorrowful, highly emotional announce
ment of Kathy's passing at the closing General Meeting of the
146th Convention on Sunday morning, August 20, 1989. An
otherwise motivational and highly productive Convention drew
to a
terribly sad close. So too did Kathleen M. McGlone's
inspirational and highly productive relationship with Psi Up
silon.
On Wednesday, August 25, 1989, Kathy's family, Psi Upsilon
and her local community said goodby for the last time at a
fiineral service held near Kathy's home in West Chester, Penn
sylvania. Over 400 people were in attendance. At the com
mencement of the service, all of the Psi Upsilon brothers in
attendance joined together and touchingly sang "Dear Old
Shrine."
It is impossible to list all of the individual accomplishments
Kathy achieved during her brief tenure as Psi U's Executive
Director. The impact of her work will be with us for many
years to come. Suffice it to say that Kathy was able to continue
the momentum that she had been instrumental in building to
transform Psi Upsilon into the modern and strong organization
that we are proud to be members of today. In writing this
article it was difficult to determine exactly what Kathy would
most like to be remembered for. She had a profound effect
upon the operations ofthe Intemational Office. Today Psi Up
silon is run with efficient time and money saving methods. Our
chapters receive visits from Field Directors personally chosen
and trained by Kathy. Our undergraduates may avail them
selves on a wealth of services and resources that became avail
able through Kathy's leadership. Our alumni receive an award
winning magazine published regularly. It is indeed difficult to
imagine that one person had such a profound impact upon Psi
Upsilon in such a short period of time.
The effect Kathy had on the tone of the International Office
was dramatic. Psi Upsilon has not been, and may never be,
able to establish compensation for employees that is in any way
competitive. Prior to Kathy's entrance upon the scene, the
entrance to the Paoli office could have been described as a
revolving door. Under Kathy's leadership, staff attrition dropped
to zero. The job of Field Director is a difficult and often thank
less one. Largely because of Kathy, not one Field Director has
ever left before his term expired. A poll of past Field Directors
would clearly indicate that Kathy was enormously responsible
for the satisfaction they derived from their year or two on the
staff. She was always there with a kind word, a bit of advice,
and a fiinny story. She treated every Field Director as a unique
combination of a colleague, a son and a special friend, which
helped make the job wonderful.
No story of Kathy's life would be complete without men
tioning her devotion to her family. While growing up, Kathy
learned about the importance offamily. But rather than reserve
such treatment to those whom she was related by blood, Kathy
treated everyone she met as a member of her own family. She
was however, a truly model parent. Being the mother of three
boys, all close in age, and being the chief executive officer of
a fairly large and complex organization, as well as dealing with
the effects of a complicated and life threatening disease, was
certainly not an easy task. Kathy seemed to master each of
these. Her day would begin before the sun came out, straight
ening the house or preparing dinner. She would have to go
have blood test at least three days a week, before going
to work at the office. She would work, often late, at the In
ternational Office but still be home virtually every night to
serve a fine meal. Weekends were a luxury; when Kathy was
not working in the office, or traveling for the Fraternity, she
got to sleep in till 7 a.m. and go to the supermarket. Her three
boys are all fine students and athletes. She made it a point to
see almost every baseball, football, hockey or whatever game
they played, and monitored their studies as well. Jerry, Jr. will
finish college at Shippensburg University in Pennsylvania this
year. Sean has begun college at the Costal Carolina College of
the University of South Carolina, and Chris has begun college
at The Johns Hopkins University in Maryland. Kathy found
that wonderful midpoint where she respected her children as
individuals to make their own decisions, but was always there
to provide guidance. She was also a devoted wife, daughter,
and sister. In fact, ber siblings jokingly fought over who would
have the honor of supplying their bone marrow to Kathy for
the transplant.
Kathy was always amused when she heard about people who
did not know her well and assumed that she was some type of
radical feminist. What Kathy did believe in was the sanctity
and integrity of all people. As a woman in the sixties, Kathy
was not given the opportunity to join Psi Upsilon, or any other
fraternity. But that fact never had any effect on her devotion
to Psi U. Kathy believed in young people, and Psi U was her
forum to make a difference. Kathy never sought to force the
issue of her gender upon our traditionally all-male organization.
Rather, Psi Upsilon's need for Kathy's enormous capabilities
forced our Fraternity to grapple with the issue so she could
continue to help us grow. She loved the Fratemity, its tradi
tions, and its members. Kathy won over everyone she met with
her charm, wisdom, sincerity, and warmth.
The Executive Directors of the fifty seven national and in
ternational fraternities are members of a very active profes
sional association called the Fraternity Executive's Association.
It would not be an exaggeration to admit that Kathy was not
entirely welcomed into this formerly all-male club. Her ap
pointment raised more than a few eyebrows. It was however,

by an undergraduate delegate to the 146th
Convention for presenting back to his
chapter what took place at the Conven
tion. Some editing has been done.
Thursday, August 17th
My plane was late (what else is
new) . . . but getting to the hotel was
relatively easy. When registering for the
Convention, we were given an enormous
amount of material to digest. It was all
in a large black binder with the Conven
tion insignia on the front. I didn't know
that there would be so much going on.
The Hyatt Regency Chicago is an enor
mous hotel, and beautiful too. Psi U cer
tainly does things right �
this place is
great. The Convention was called to or
der Thursday evening, I didn't really un
derstand what was going on in the meet
ing, it was all procedural-type things.
William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega '66,
President of the Executive Council, ran
the meeting. An interesting woman
named Patti Holmes (and not bad looking
either!), gave a motivational talk called
"Building an Attitude of Excellence."
Following Patti's presentation we were
all taken by bus to the Epsilon Omega
Chapter house. It was a modem house,
which I didn't expect, and very large.
The dinner served was based on a theme
called "A Taste of Chicago," with various
Chicago-oriented offerings, ranging from
ribs to deep dish pizza. The food was
FANTASTIC. I had an opportunity to
talk with many Brothers from other chap
ters and it was quite interesting to hear
what it is like at the different schools. \
Following the dinner, I went out with a
bunch ofguys who knew the Chicago area.
Friday, August 18th
Well somehow, someway I made my
committee meeting. The wake up came
very early, it seemed like I'd just gone
to bed! I was on the Budget and Devel
opment Committee. I learned a great deal
From top to bottom: 1) Convention attendees
boarding the bus for the Epsilon Omega
Chapter house and the "A Taste of Chicago"
dinner. 2) Plentiful food and good company
at the dinner. 3) Nelson J. Leidner, Jr., Pi
'70; John K. Menzies, Pi '41; Jonathan C.
Piper, Pi '87; Michael G. Barton, Pi '91; and
Douglas S. Sweeny, Pi '90 participate in the
festivities sponsored by the Epsilon Omega.
4) Undergraduates and alumni alike enjoyed
the festive atmosphere at the Epsilon Omega
Chapter house.

Annual Giving to Psi Upsilon 1988 -
1989

November, 1989
Dear Brothers:
It is with great pleasure that we report on the success of the
1988-89 Annual Giving Program. A total of 2,436 loyal members
of Psi Upsilon donated $155,685. This represents an average gift
of $63.91.
This generosity has enabled the opportunities that membership
in Psi Upsilon offers to be extended to another generation of fine
undergraduates.
The following record of statistics and lists represent gifts re
ceived from July 1, 1988 through June 30, 1989 (gifts received
subsequent to June 30, have been credited to the 1989-90 pro
gram). The cumulative total of contributions which an alumnus
has made to the Annual Giving Program since its inception in
1964 is recognized through various giving levels. The names in
bolder print represent leadership contributors (1988-89 gifts of
$50 or more). Years of consecutive giving are shown in paren
theses after the name and class of the donor.
Many of Psi Upsilon's loyal donors for the first time received
a telephone call from an undergraduate member as a part of this
year's solicitation program. The telethon worked quite well and
the Executive Council is deeply appreciative to those under
graduates that donated their time to making it such a success.
We are fortunate to have such faithful and generous alumni.
On behalf of the Executive Council, thank you!
Yours in the bonds,
William R. Robie, Epsilon Omega '66
President

Carl A. Beck, Delta '41 was elected

ofknowledge to this post from his notable

ton University, Brother Beck transferred

Jersey), and a former director of the Peoples National Bank of Norristown,

Society for the Advancement of Management; a seminar leader, lecturer, and
panelist for the American Management Association; and a seminar leader for
the Council for Intemational Progress in Management in La Paz, Bolivia.
Brother Beck has been involved in a variety of professional and civic activities.
His principal interests have included the American National Metric Council of
which he is currently the Chairman and the National Small Business United,
having served as Chairman from 1966-70. Other interests have included the
Rotary Club, the King of Prussia (Pennsylvania) Chamber of Commerce, the
Child Development Center of Norristown, Pennsylyania, the Manufacturers
Association ofthe Delaware Valley. He is a former Director ofthe Delta Chapter
Alumni Corporation.
He is a member ofthe Union League (Philadelphia), the Philadelphia County
Club, Little Egg Harbor Yacht Club, The Corinthians, the US Power Squadron,
the Nassau Club (Princeton, New Jersey), and the Princeton Club of New York.
Brother Beck and his wife Florence make their home in Bala Cynwood, Penn
sylvania.
